newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB opposes hasty IMF gold sales.
newsitem.headline: SNB opposes hasty IMF gold sales.

text.p: Swiss National Bank (SNB) president Hans Meyer said that the Swiss central bank was opposed to over-hasty gold sales by the International Monetary Fund to help poor countries.
In an interview published by Swiss press agency SDA published on Friday, Meyer said that such a step, aimed at reducing debt of poor countries, requires thorough analysis.
The IMF needs large reserves in view of the possible risks tied to Eastern Europe and Latin America, he said.
An SNB spokesman said the interview was conducted on Wednesday in Switzerland before Meyer departed for IMF and World Bank meetings in Washington.
Switzerland is not seeking to stand in the way of discussions about the role of gold in the world economy.
But, together with other countries, Switzerland is sceptical about recommendations for a speedy solution to help poorer countries by over-rash gold sales, Meyer said.
The topic is likely to be brought up in talks at the IMF in the coming week, and is also likely to resurface at the IMF's autumn meeting, he said.
At the same time, however, Meyer also said the Swiss central bank plans to reduce its very high gold reserves.

The Swiss government and the SNB already said in March that a plan to revalue the SNB's gold reserves would free up seven billion Swiss francs. The government has proposed to use that amount as a basis to create a humanitarian fund.
The fund, which is tied to constitutional reforms governing the SNB's management of its assets, still requires approval of the Swiss parliament and a public referendum.
Meyer said that the SNB's reserve "cushion" which has been built up in the last years is more than adequate.
Today, the SNB's gold holdings are equal to those of Germany, which is 10 times larger than Switzerland.
The Netherlands holds only half as large an amount as Switzerland.

Even after revaluation and separation of a portion of its gold reserves, it would still have gold valued at 18 billion Swiss francs. In addition, reserves for currency risks are currently about 30 billion francs, about five billion more than the recommended value.
